summary:
SYNAPSE is a prototype health-monitoring interface for astronauts on long missions, built by Team 3S (Synapse Space Systems).

We developed a modular system in a microservices architecture. The prototype runs on synthetic data, gathering health indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, glucose, sleep, radiation dose and cabin CO2, etc.). It translates complex data into a user-friendly, interactive interface (what needs action now, what is due, is it urgent, what the problem is and how to understand it). A turnable body map with anatomical layers shows which exact part of the body is concerned. Colour codes, alert signs, checklists and self-checks keep the user engaged and enables a visual understanding of the issue. Each alert states its urgency and one next step, with explanations and video demonstrations where necessary.

The system lets the user with no medical expertise evaluate their own health and act on it in due time. Our “lazy astronaut” hypothesis helps determine data and UX/UI design hierarchy by importance. Diversity and inclusiveness are considered in the personalisation features. We privileged the use of plain language, so the action point is clear even under stress, without unnecessary distractions. The hard data runs on the background for reporting and tracking purposes. It may be consulted but does not show on the primary screen which focusses on the system's  direct communication and relationship with the user.
details:
What it does and how it works
SYNAPSE is a prototype interface that gathers an astronaut’s health indicators and shows, on one screen, action points, recommendations and explanations. Each reading is judged against three references: the user’s own pre-flight baseline, their recent norm in the current environment, and a published standard. A turnable body map with anatomical layers marks any system outside its expected range. Every alert states its urgency and one next step, including when the instrument likely to affect health monitoring is deficient or dysfunctional. Trends cover every indicator over time, beside real NASA measurements of radiation dose and cabin CO2 from the International Space Station. Instrument guides, plain-language explanations and a voice assistant, EVO, add on layers all designed to ensure that the user gets the message by all possible means. The prototype runs on synthetic crew data.

Benefits
A lay user with no medical expertise can evaluate their own health and act on it autonomously. Information is ordered by importance and presented in a language that the user elects (written and spoken languages may differ), all in plain language. Status is shown by colour and signs. Modules can be personalised beforehand and at any time to suit the user's preferences. The AI Assistant (EVO) with vocal features adds a double verification layer just in case the visual screen alert signs go unnoticed. It can also be personalised to add a gamification element and make the experience more personal.

Intended impact
Safer and more autonomous long-duration missions, where communication delays make immediate self help impossible. With the user’s consent, a structured record could also support space-medicine research, training and follow-up after return. In case of unexpected accidents or death of the user during space missions, and provided the user's contextual consent, the data can be used to identify the source of any accident, pathology, during investigations, or simply be shared with family members to make the cause of the incident known.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one self-contained file, with SVG drawings and no external libraries. Python for the build script and for processing the NASA data tables. Node.js, jsdom and Playwright with Chrome for automated testing. GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. No hardware: instrument readings are simulated. AI tools used: Claude Code, Canva and Grok, as disclosed in the AI field.

How it is creative
Our “lazy astronaut” hypothesis: design for a tired, stressed user who must still get the right action first time, and keep raw data in the background until it is needed. A 3D body map built entirely in code, with layers and a prosthesis option. Playful features (a logging streak, a recorded journey) that all serve a purpose: keeping the crew member engaged, tracking and incentivising a cognitive "active status", and countering isolation.

Factors we considered
Scientific reliability (every threshold has a named source, and gaps are stated). Accessibility, inclusiveness and diversity (astronauts of any gender, age, size, disability or neurotype). Data privacy (data stays on the device, sharing is off by default, consent features are integrated). Legal and regulatory requirements (authorisations, compliance, responsibility). Business development, financial risk control and mitigation, and economic viability (modular architecture embedding integrated microservices allows deployment in phases and global collaboration).
